fixes.explanation: Ezra the priest is facedown before the house of God, and a very large assembly of Israelites gathers around him. The text says men, women and children (Ezra 10:1). One man on the ground praying, and then a crowd gathers. I think that's a lot of people to find around you when you lift your head.

Small is the one word that doesn't fit here. Ezra the priest is praying when a very large assembly of Israelites gathers around him (Ezra 10:1). The text says it includes men, women and children. If I tried to bake for that crowd, I'd run out of dough before the second row.
Babylon isn't mentioned in this promise. Shecaniah says, “…we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (Ezra 10:4). That's a promise of support for Ezra, not a trip anywhere.

Swear is the word. Ezra gets up and makes the leading priests, Levites and all Israel take an oath to do what had been said, and they took the oath (Ezra 10:5). An oath is a serious promise made before God, not a casual nod.

That's right. While Ezra stays in the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib, he eats no food and drinks no water (Ezra 10:6). The text says he's mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles. No food, no water, just mourning.
Forty days? Friend, that's thirteen times too much time. The text says whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property (Ezra 10:8). Three days, and then the consequences.

That's the consequence. Whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). The text says this was according to the counsel of the leaders and elders. That's a serious deadline.

No trip to Babylon in this verse, friend. The text says whoever failed to appear within three days would forfeit all his property and be expelled from the assembly of the exiles (Ezra 10:8). So he'd lose everything he owned and his place in the assembly, with no moving truck involved.

The heavy rain. On the twentieth day of the ninth month, the people sit in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). So they're trembling over the matter and the heavy rain at the same time. I think that's a rough combination.

The text doesn't mention any wind. It says the people sat in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain (Ezra 10:9). Rain is the only weather the verse names. Sitting in a square in that? I'd have been asking where the roof was.

That's not what they suggest. The assembly proposes that their leaders represent the whole assembly, and that everyone in their towns who has married a foreign woman come at an appointed time (Ezra 10:14). The elders and judges of each town come along too. So it's a plan built on towns and leaders, not each family on its own.

Waiting for the rainy season to end isn't what they propose. The assembly says, “Let our leaders represent the whole assembly.” Then each town's men come at an appointed time with the elders and judges of that town (Ezra 10:14). So the plan is built on leaders and appointed times.

Judges is right. The men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). So each town sends its own elders and judges along with the men concerned. That's a town-by-town setup.

No soldiers are named. The assembly says each town's men come at an appointed time, “…together with the elders and judges of each town…” (Ezra 10:14). Judges are the ones named along with the elders. It's elders and judges in this plan, with no soldiers in sight.

The rain is real, but it's not what they want turned away. They say the plan goes on “…until the fierce anger of our God in this matter is turned away from us.” (Ezra 10:14). They had just mentioned the rainy season as a reason for the plan (Ezra 10:13). But the thing they name as turned away is God's fierce anger.

Singers aren't what the text names, friend. It says Ezra the priest selected men who were family heads, each of them identified by name, to represent their families (Ezra 10:16). Singers do show up later in the list of men (Ezra 10:24). These men speak for their families.
